title: Why depth helps
summary: One wide hidden layer can approximate any continuous function, but it pays for every wiggle with its own neurons. Depth reuses work: a two-neuron tent folds the interval, and composing it L times gives 2^L straight pieces, which a single layer would need about 2^L neurons to match.
llm_link: A language model is a deep stack of blocks, each refining every token's vector a little further, building on what earlier blocks computed rather than starting from scratch.
key_ideas: Universal approximation: one hidden layer with enough neurons can approximate any continuous function on a bounded region.
With one input, n ReLU neurons in one layer make at most n + 1 straight pieces: one corner per neuron.
The tent t(x) = 2·ReLU(x) − 4·ReLU(x − ½) folds [0, 1] in half onto itself.
Composing the tent L times gives 2^L pieces with only 2L neurons; a single layer needs about 2^L neurons for the same function.
Depth lets features build on features (edges → parts → objects), at the price of signals that must pass through every layer.

quiz.q: What does the universal approximation theorem promise?
options: One hidden layer with enough neurons can approximate any continuous function on a bounded region
A single neuron can approximate any function
quiz.explain: It is an existence result about width: it says nothing about how many neurons you need or how to find their weights.

quiz.q: Predict the result: with t(x) = 2x for x ≤ ½ and 2 − 2x for x > ½, what is t(t(0.3))?
How many straight pieces does the tent applied four times have on [0, 1]?
A single hidden layer of 50 ReLU neurons reads one input. At most how many straight pieces can its output have?
quiz.explain: Each neuron adds at most one corner, so 50 corners split the line into at most 51 pieces.

quiz.q: Why do language models stack dozens of blocks instead of using one enormous block?
options: Wide layers cannot be trained on GPUs
Each block can build on what earlier blocks computed, reusing work instead of paying for every pattern separately
Depth reduces the number of parameters to zero
quiz.explain: Like the folds in this lesson, later blocks refine representations earlier ones already built.

problems.title: The tent and its folds
problems.prompt:
Write tent(x) using only relu (two neurons): it should be 2x on [0, ½] and 2 − 2x on [½, 1]. Then write fold(x, k) that applies the tent k times, like a network k layers deep.

tent(0.25) == 0.5, tent(0.75) == 0.5
fold(0.3, 2) == 0.8

tests.name: tent values
fold twice
tests.code:
got = fold(0.3, 2)
assert abs(got - 0.8) < 1e-9, f'tent(0.3) = 0.6 and tent(0.6) = 0.8, got {got}'

tests.name: fold zero times is the identity
tests.code: assert fold(0.37, 0) == 0.37, 'applying the tent zero times should return x unchanged'

tests.name: folds stay inside [0, 1]
tests.code:
vals = [fold(i / 97, 5) for i in range(98)]
assert all(-1e-9 <= v <= 1 + 1e-9 for v in vals), 'the tent maps [0, 1] onto [0, 1], so every fold should stay inside it'

hints: The slope must change by -4 at x = 0.5: subtract 4 * relu(x - 0.5).
fold: for _ in range(k): x = tent(x)

problems.title: Count the straight pieces
problems.prompt:
Write count_pieces(f, n=4096): sample f at x = i/n for i = 0..n, compute the slope between neighbouring samples, and count how many straight pieces there are (one more than the number of times the slope changes).

Then check the claim from the video: count_pieces(lambda x: fold(x, k)) should be 2k. The starter includes tent and fold.

tests.name: a straight line is one piece
tests.code:
got = count_pieces(lambda x: 3 * x + 1)
assert got == 1, f'a straight line has 1 piece, got {got}'

tests.name: one tent is two pieces
tests.code:
got = count_pieces(tent)
assert got == 2, f'the tent goes up then down: 2 pieces, got {got}'

tests.name: pieces double with each fold

hints: slopes = [(ys[i + 1] - ys[i]) * n for i in range(n)]
changes = sum(1 for a, b in zip(slopes, slopes[1:]) if abs(a - b) > 1e-6)

problems.title: Neuron budget: deep versus wide
problems.prompt:
Write neurons_needed(pieces), returning two numbers for a target number of straight pieces that is a power of two:

  • deep: neurons used by stacking tents (2 per layer, and L layers give 2L pieces)
  • wide: the fewest neurons a single hidden layer needs (n neurons give at most n + 1 pieces)
neurons_needed(1024)   # (20, 1023)
problems.starter:
import math

def neurons_needed(pieces):
    # TODO: L = log2(pieces); deep = 2 * L; wide = pieces - 1
    deep = 0
    wide = 0
    return deep, wide

tests.name: ten layers
tests.code:
got = neurons_needed(1024)
assert tuple(got) == (20, 1023), f'1024 = 2**10: 10 layers x 2 = 20 deep neurons, and 1023 wide ones; got {got}'

tests.name: one tent
tests.code:
got = neurons_needed(2)
assert tuple(got) == (2, 1), f'2 pieces: one tent (2 neurons) or a single ReLU (1 neuron); got {got}'

tests.name: deep grows slowly
tests.code:
d20, w20 = neurons_needed(2 ** 20)
assert d20 == 40 and w20 == 2 ** 20 - 1, f'20 layers: 40 deep neurons vs {2 ** 20 - 1} wide ones; got {(d20, w20)}'
assert isinstance(d20, int), f'return whole numbers, not {type(d20).__name__} (round the log, or use bit_length)'

hints: L = round(math.log2(pieces)), or pieces.bit_length() - 1 for an exact power of two.
problems.solution:
import math

def neurons_needed(pieces):
    L = pieces.bit_length() - 1
    deep = 2 * L
    wide = pieces - 1
    return deep, wide
